## $1 Million Dollar Challenge Complete! Ross's Trade Recap

Two-and-a-half-year challenge turning $583 into $1 million profit over 553 trading days. Executed 2,873 total trades with 67% accuracy at $1.8k average daily profit using 9,000 share position size. Stock selection focused on $2-$10 price range with catalyst-driven moves and low float. Entry strategies emphasized gaps 10%+ with news catalysts. Exit discipline required taking "base hits" rather than holding for larger moves. Daily routine: trade only 9:30-10:30 AM window. Strategy was finding "one stock per day" with big move potential rather than scalp trading. Monthly profit-taking: never kept more than $50-75k at any time. [ACCT]: Final stages showed emotional pressure from being close to goal—overtrading, larger share sizes, FOMO trading. Recovery required refocusing on actual stock charts rather than P&L numbers.

## $11,734.61 in 2hrs of Day Trading

Morning session yielding $11,735 profit. Market slower than recent days but found opportunity through catalyst-driven setup. Stock criteria: $2-$10 price, sub-1M float, reverse split history, news catalyst required. Pre-market scanning identified BATL (+200%) and OCG but avoided BATL due to: heavy pre-market volume (50M shares), thick spreads, multiple false breakouts suggesting weakening momentum. Key trade NVE on breaking news (patent approval): sub-1M float check, reverse split check passed. Entry on micro pullback at 290, targeting break of 300. Trade executed from 290→560, micro pullbacks provided re-entry points. Pattern recognition: dip trades working well when MACD positive. Stopped momentum trading when MACD turned negative and sellers stacked heavily (25-30k share blocks). Risk management: big sellers on news suggest insider selling/dilution—flagged as warning sign. Deliberately missed BATL's 385% move to lock profits. [ACCT]: Daily goal is $5k; crossed threshold and locked profits at 2-hour mark to avoid overtrading.

## $18k in 30 minutes with this Day Trading Strategy

Morning session trading first 30 minutes, netting $18k on WETG (weather group stock). Context: 185-to-1 reverse split Friday; adjusted float under 1M post-split. Catalyst: breaking news 8:30 AM on AI application launch. Stock met all five core criteria: (1) up 10%+ at entry (already +35%), (2) relative volume 5x-6x, (3) fresh news (AI buzzword), (4) price $2-$20 range ($12-13 entry), (5) float under 10M. Entry timing: first trade at $12+ for break of $12.50; bought 4,000 shares (2,000 at 11.71, added 2,000 at 11.97), sold 3,000 at 12.13. Micro pullbacks on 10-second chart showed quick consolidations; entry was "first pullback to break previous high" setup. Scalp mentality: taking green immediately, focusing base hits over home runs. Trade sequence: (1) entry 12.13 profit; (2) dip 12.34, added 2,000; (3) dip 12.96, added 1,500; (4) break 14, sold position; (5) dip trade 13.07, added 4,500 for move to 14; (6) micro pullback 14.40, added 1,500 for retest; (7) momentum candle 1,000 shares at 15.94, stopped near 15.70. Price: 12→13→14→15→16→17→18→19.16 (halt). Volume surge into 1,650 triggered halt; resumed 1,875, final trade 19.15. Total: $18,538 in under 2 hours. Risk management: reduced position size as price extended (4k shares→1.5k at highs) due to wider spreads and higher volatility. [ACCT]: Trading main account; managed risk by reducing size as stock became extended; acknowledged final trades risky and stopped before open halts created dangerous conditions.

## $195 Million OVERNIGHT Fortune on a China Stock

Primarily editorial and fundamental analysis rather than trade-level decision making. Chinese stock TWG moved $2 pre-market to $6+ intraday after announcing $10.8M secondary offering at $0.40/share. Irrational market behavior: typically offerings crash stocks, but TWG squeezed higher as shorts covered. Company financials disconnect: $16M revenue, $5M gross profit, $2M net profit; valuation jumped from $20M to $200M+ market cap. Trader position: minimal—pre-market dip trade at $3.50, added at 4, peaked $4.40-4.50, stopped scaling due to spoof order concerns (40k buyer wall disappeared on dips). Cautious entry: drew ascending support line, waited retest, entered break-back over 3.50, added through 4-5 range with max position 10k shares. Restraint reasons: (1) spoof order red flag, (2) offering dilution ($27M new shares at $0.40), (3) Chinese stock history of pump-dumps, (4) asymmetric risk/reward post-$5. Final profit: $548 on small-sized trades; deliberately avoided big squeeze from 2.70→5.18 (100% in 40 seconds). Discipline: walked away at daily goal ($5k Friday) rather than chase parabolic move. [ACCT]: Deliberate position sizing due to high risk perception; stopped trading at daily goal to avoid overexposure to suspicious activity; emotional restraint overrode FOMO on 100% parabolic move.

## $23K in 3 Days of Trading! Ross' Trade Recap

Three-day week totaling $23,000 profit ($5k Wed, $8k Thu, $10k Fri). Thursday and Friday showed strong winning trade clustering as market heated up. Gap scanner strategy: stock criteria included 5%+ gap, price under $10, news catalyst, volume 5x average, historically small float. Wednesday ($5k): GELS; first trade at 7 AM set early cushion. Thursday ($8k): described as best green day of month; momentum-driven market cluster. Friday ($10k): $26,553 total (exceeding $5k goal significantly). Key trades: FFEN early entry, CGA ($240, minimal), FF HL major on first 5-min candle to new high, multiple dip trades adding at support. FF HL trace: opened $3.50, pulled back $3.26-3.30, broke 3.50→4.19 in early spike. Trader hesitated on first 3.50 break, waited confirmation, entered on retest. Built position 3,000→6,000-9,000 through multiple adds. Managed risk by leaving money if spreads widened or volume declined. Price targets: retest of previous day highs, acceptance above key levels (3.50, 4.00, 4.50, 5.00, 6.00). Halts strategy: first candle to make new high off halt = re-entry signal. Volatility through opens: waited confirmation before hitting big positions. Exit: locked profits before 10 AM threshold; gave back some gains on false breaks (-$500 twice) but stayed ahead. Weekly: 1-hour trading window (9:30-10:30 AM), cumulative $25k week. [ACCT]: Strong weeks cluster together; trader manages emotions by focusing base hits over home runs; gave back small amounts late in session but remained disciplined about total P&L; comfortable with profit-taking approach rather than max-profit extraction.

## $26,553.22 on a 100% Squeeze on Breaking News

Single-day $26,553 profit from breaking news catalyst. Market context: tariff volatility; three-day cumulative $40k+. Two main trades: SNOA (small winner $2k after two-way trade, up 100% pre-market); ENSC (major carrier of profit). SNOA: gapped 100% pre-market but already heavily moved; first scalp $1,000 on low-quality setup, second trade loss -$400. Exited early citing choppiness, moved to scanner watch. **ENSC primary driver**: Breaking news 8 AM on US patent for opiate use disorder treatment. Bio-tech, low-float, news catalyst = ideal. Entry: scanner hit at 2.90 triggered micro pullback pattern; bought 2,900 at break of 3.00. Scaled aggressively: 2.90 break→3.44, micro pullback→re-entered for 3.50 break→4.00. Added at 4.00 break, topped 4.20 with small profit, pulled back. Re-entered dip 3.80, added more 3.80-4.05. Strong move through 4.50-4.60, longer pullback formed cup-and-handle. Bought dip 4.50, held into 5.00 break, added 4.43 for max position 4,500 shares. Price: 2.90→3.00→3.50→4.00→4.50→5.20 (pre-halt peak). Extended move 4.60 with volume surge marked "front of move" vs "back of move". MACD positive throughout main squeeze, turned negative near highs = exit signal. Divergence: MACD bearish while price attempted 4.50-5.00 resistance; opted not to chase into weakness. Secondary entry post-MACD negative failed; dips weren't deep for quality entry. Halt down bounce wasn't big enough to re-engage. Total $26,553 despite missing extended afternoon move. Risk management: reduced size into parabolic (front-loaded early when MACD confirmed, de-risked when failed). [ACCT]: Better early cushion from SNOA allowing more risk on ENSC; maintained discipline by walking away when patterns weakened despite stock making new highs; acknowledged missing extended move but protected profit.

CNET: attempted 4.50 entry (no fill), stock tapped 4.80, pulled back. Partial fill 4.71-4.74, sold 4.79-4.70 for $450 profit. Saw 60k seller at 4.80, opted out rather than fight supply. FEN: aggressive 10k shares on scanner; squeezed 2.65, came back 2.20, stopped -$200. Halts pausing market; resumes unpredictable. ARC ON (archeon): dipped 3.10, re-entered 3.20, dipped again. First trade +$107, second dip trade (2,500 anticipating new high) lost -$250. Total +$789. LEDS (light emitting): halted on circuit breaker (>10% in 5 min), waited resume, pullback then entry. [ACCT]: Emotional frustration from internet issues forced deliberate slowdown; frustration normally leads to aggressive risk-taking ("punch a pillow" mentality) but consciously de-risked by reducing share size; acknowledged being frustrated makes him trade "like a jerk"; needs internal presence of mind to pull back when emotions run high; travel/location stress affected focus.

## $3,234.38 in 1hr on the 35th Day of 2018!

Reentry: stock pulled back, re-entered 7,500 shares at 9.00 targeting prior day's 11.00 high. Aggressive scaling: added at 9.21, 9.25, 9.46, 9.70, 9.88 (pyramid on way up). Total shares 45k. Sold through move at 9.40, 9.60, 9.80, up to 10.20. Position mechanics: "add and sell" style—adds on strength, takes partial profits, re-adds on dips. ZZZZ final profit: $3,356. Secondary ARCA: attempted entry anticipating halt squeeze, entered late 6.77, sold 7.25 for $300 profit. Final trade loser -$422. Note swing trade alert (TYLER/MNK): bullish flag entry $20.50 for break, first target $21.50 hit in 30 min (template for beginners—easier than aggressive day trading). Key insight: day trading requires speed, confidence, tight hotkeys. Swing trading more forgiving with less pressure. Account context: started year $33k, now $399k (crossing $400k tomorrow). 2017 profit: $391k. Daily average: $10.8k/day. Monthly run-rate: $229k. Goal: need $160k more for $1M by Q1 end. [ACCT]: Still red $7,200 on month of February; consciously managing not to blow account or feel monthly goal pressure; focusing on week-by-week and month-by-month averages rather than daily targets; acknowledges slower months will come and big months must cover them.

## $3.6K on The 36th Trading Day! Ross' Trade Recap

Day 36 of 2018, +$3,636 profit (trader calls it "lucky number"). Intentional trade quality focus: came in seeking to finish green only (not chasing yesterday's loss), which improved performance. **Early cushion FTNW**: gapped 200% pre-market, strong catalyst; opened 3.50, jumped for 4.50 break. Hesitated on dip 3.20 (feared washout), waited confirmation. Entry 3.40 (partial), added 3.57, 3.86, 3.89, 3.97, averaged higher. Sold 4.06, 3.99, then bought dip 3.10, added 3.13, exited 3.24-3.26. Profit: $2,121 first trade. Secondary: TL +$600; EV +$800. Short attempt (READ): tried short at 3.00 anticipating resistance bounce; stock squeezed 3.25, stopped at gap 3.25. Loss -$390 (damage control; could have been worse). Small scalp EV second entry after pullback, minor loss. Avoided overtrading: on quality-focused days with fewer trades, P&L improves. All trades off gap scanner. Three base hits = green day. Sim account commentary: reviewed student accounts trading FUV, CIFS, FTNW; many students trading 1M+ shares (overtrading noted); some unrealized losses exceeding $70k. Advice: tighter discipline needed with real money; practice sim aggressively, then switch to real. YTD stats: up $136k in 36 days ($3,794/day average). Full-year projection: at $3,700/day = $850k. Conservative estimate using 2017 average $2,117/day = $535k (exceeds $500k goal). Need for goal: only $1,873/day (well below pace). [ACCT]: Dual accounts (IRA +$491, main -$442 net); tracking above annual goal; aware $3.7k daily average inflated by strong Jan-Feb and slower months will follow; emphasizes big months building cushion for slow; 2017 had two red months (April, September) but finished $370k.

- Gap-and-go dynamics: Morning window (7-11am) = highest probability; afternoon light volume = spreads widen, hard to manage

- IPO volatility (PIK, SBET): Spreads and micro-reversals require small position sizing; exits into reversals > holds through exhaustion
- Live morning shows teach real-time decision-making: Scanner alerts (ADTX, NXTP), level-2 confirmation, halt logic
- Meme-stock avoidance: Below 200 MA + high-risk names in bear markets = discipline over FOMO
- Private-placement catalysts: Entry on news, scale strength, trim into reversals (Vitalik $SBET example)

- Green-day preservation > big-win chasing (bear market adjustment: $500-3K daily goals vs. $5K historic)
- Position sizing discipline: 1K-5K shares typical, oversizing into resistance = trap risk
- Morning-window optimization: Exit by 10:30-11am if targets hit (afternoon spreads widen unpredictably)
- Self-awareness protocol: Headaches, frustration, short fuse = STOP immediately (FILE 88 $OLB example)

Educational episode on algo flush mechanics using PEV example (dropped $8.28→$7.40 in one candle, halted down). Key teaching: understand order matching, high-frequency trading algo response, and risk models to read market structure. Not a trade—a framework for understanding mechanical price moves vs. fundamental news.

Switched to more conservative approach when ADTX ABCD pattern emerged around daily resistance: small 2K share starter, properly managed escalation as pattern proved itself. Net day: +$800 final after other small scalps filled gaps. Key learning: algo spikes on news can't be traded profitably (market makers protecting risk), topping tails are real warning signals (not to be ignored for bigger payoff hope), position sizing discipline tighter when already down from losses, need to lock profits higher on ABCD pattern completions rather than adding final positions.

[SIGNAL: CODX gap-and-go continuation, break 18 premarket resistance with momentum] → [EXIT: Halted going down at 16.19, cut at 15.50-15.60 on resumption pop] → [RESULT: Down -$6,500 total, watched stock rip to 19.67 minutes later] → [LOSS / Timing trap]

[SIGNAL: APT strong headline + break of premarket high at 20.47 while CODX halted] → [EXIT: Also immediately halted at 18.00, set stop at low, filled at 17.50 with slippage] → [RESULT: Down -$7,000 total, stock bounced to 21 after exit] → [LOSS / Second halt shock]

[SIGNAL: Lesson reflection - three stocks halted going down simultaneously at open] → [EXIT: Risk management held firm; did not average down despite max-loss trigger] → [RESULT: Avoided $30K+ catastrophic stacking loss by cutting both positions quickly] → [WIN / Loss containment]

[SIGNAL: Month resilience check] → [EXIT: Despite -$14,500 red day, month remains strong] → [RESULT: Up $70,000 for month (vs $87,000 before trade)] → [PARTIAL WIN / Maintains green month]

**Session Summary:**
An exceptionally challenging red day marked by unprecedented market conditions. Three coronavirus-sympathy stocks gapped up 50-80% premarket, triggering Ross's core gap-and-go strategy at market open. CODX and APT both executed near-identical breakout setups—entries at premarket resistance breaks with tight risk targets. However, within 60 seconds of his entries, both stocks experienced circuit-breaker halts going down, a scenario Ross hadn't encountered in his entire trading career. CODX dropped from 17.76 entry to 16.19 halt level; APT followed suit immediately after. On resumption, both stocks continued lower before eventually bouncing back to target zones, but Ross had already exited with -$6,500 and -$7,000 losses respectively. The critical decision to cut both positions—rather than average down or hold through multi-halt scenarios—prevented a potential $30,000+ catastrophic loss. On resumption, he cut losses at $15.40, crystallizing approximately a -$7,000 loss. While still holding CODX in halt-down status, he initiated a second identical setup on APT at $20.47, but experienced the same shock: a halt-down at $18. With no averaging-down option (already at max loss threshold), he stopped out at $17.50 with slippage for another -$7,000 loss. A third stock (VIR) also halted, compounding the day's frustration. Both trades would have been profitable within minutes of resumption, but holding through dual halts going down exposed unacceptable risk of 30%+ declines. By 9:35 AM, he had hit his max daily loss and was sidelined for the remainder of the session. Despite the devastating start, his disciplined decision to cut losses rather than average down prevented potential catastrophic losses.

SUMMARY:
This episode explores the phenomenon of Chinese IPOs making extraordinary moves, particularly HKD which climbed from $12 to $2,555 (13,000%+) and other IPOs regularly posting 2,200% first-day gains via underwriter Network One Financial. Ross examines a Bloomberg article investigating why these stocks experience such wild volatility and attributes it primarily to market-making mechanics rather than manipulation. When market makers deem small-cap IPO risk unacceptable, they withdraw from making markets, creating thin order books with abundant buyers but few sellers. This liquidity vacuum, combined with insider lockup periods that prevent supply, drives explosive upside moves. When momentum reverses, the absence of buyers on the bid creates equally dramatic downside. Ross explains his approach to trading these volatile stocks: starting with one high-conviction trade to build a profit cushion, then scaling aggressively into winners while ruthlessly cutting losers. He notes that volatility equals opportunity for breakout traders and references his early career successes trading 20-40% daily movers and 100%+ moves (DRYS, etc.). His strategy focuses on sympathy momentum—riding waves of popular small caps like HKD—while maintaining discipline about position sizing and knowing when a stock becomes too expensive to trade profitably.

Despite ending the day with max loss, Ross used the recap to analyze his metrics: 33% win rate, 4-cent average winner, 12-cent average loser. He traced four consecutive red days to the same behavioral deviation—entering extended moves without waiting for clean pullback confirmation. The market had shifted from rewarding aggressive chasing (as it did in February-March) to punishing it. Rather than fight the conditions, he committed to waiting for one-minute and five-minute pullback setups, downsizing share size, and reducing trade frequency until cleaner opportunities emerged.

The overarching theme was emotional entrapment: losing money on day one generated desperation to recoup losses on day two, which intensified the desire to size up and take bigger risks on day three. His gross profit across his trading career stood at $11+ million, yet recent bear-market months (this slowest month since November 2020) tested his discipline severely. His possible solutions included diversifying to large-cap trading (DKS example with chop and algos), options, or forex—all admittedly requiring years to master and unlikely to improve near-term profitability. His core insight: respect that cold streaks are normal, survival beats optimizing gains, and the path forward demands either extreme patience or strategic pivot into new asset classes. He emphasized that even 11M in career profit doesn't inoculate traders from drawdown cycles; the challenge remains managing psychology, sizing, and recognizing when to sit out versus when to adapt.

NO-TRADE SUMMARY:
Ross presents a detailed educational analysis of day trading in bear market conditions, addressing the challenges and adjustments required when overall market momentum is weak. He emphasizes that bear markets require a shift from trading every stock that moves to being more selective and disciplined about entry timing and setup quality. Ross discusses the importance of trading the front side of momentum moves rather than chasing extensions, noting that in choppy conditions, stocks frequently create false breakouts that trap aggressive traders. He uses specific market examples to illustrate how tight stops, smaller position sizes, and heightened caution about technical breakouts become essential. The video stresses that in bear markets, waiting for confirmed strength and avoiding stocks with recent trap history becomes critical to reducing unnecessary losses. Ross explains how individual stock selection becomes more important in bear markets since fewer overall market-wide catalysts are driving sustained momentum. He reviews market scanning methodology and emphasizes that patience—even to the point of taking entire days off from trading if no high-probability setups appear—is superior to forcing trades in choppy conditions. The presentation reinforces that successful momentum traders must adapt their approach seasonally and adjust position sizing based on market regime, maintaining discipline during periods when the overall market environment does not support aggressive trading strategies.

NO-TRADE SUMMARY:
Ross presents a comprehensive step-by-step guide to the three-day squeeze setup, a technical pattern frequently traded for momentum plays in his strategy. He explains the mechanics of how stocks undergo rapid upward moves, experience brief consolidations, and then break higher for additional legs of profit. The pattern itself emerges when a stock has climbed significantly, creates a brief pause or squeeze, and then continues higher, creating a tradeable breakout opportunity. Ross emphasizes the importance of using multiple technical confirmations, including moving average convergence divergence (MACD), volume profile analysis, and support/resistance levels, to avoid false breakouts that are common in choppy markets. He describes how to identify the setup on both daily and intraday timeframes, with the daily chart providing the broader context and the one-minute chart offering entry timing. The video covers position sizing strategy, noting that partial entries and scaling into positions during successive pullbacks allow traders to reduce risk while maintaining exposure to strong moves. Ross discusses exit strategies, emphasizing profit-taking targets based on technical resistance levels and the importance of cutting losses quickly when the pattern fails. Throughout the presentation, he stresses that this setup works best during hot market conditions with strong overall market participation, and that adapting or avoiding the setup during bear markets is essential for consistent profitability.

FILE 0791 | TYPE: No Trades
---

NO-TRADE SUMMARY:
Ross presents a detailed educational breakdown of using the MACD (Moving Average Convergence Divergence) indicator as a tool to reduce false breakout trades during choppy market conditions. He explains that MACD is a lagging indicator that tracks the relationship between two exponential moving averages, with divergence indicating momentum acceleration and convergence indicating potential consolidation or reversal. Ross describes his methodology of only trading when MACD shows positive divergence—when the indicator is above zero and moving higher—as this tends to align with the strongest momentum. During bear or choppy markets, he restricts aggressive trading to periods when MACD displays large ascending mountain ranges, avoiding entries when the indicator is negative or when moving averages are converging. Ross provides specific chart examples showing how MACD confirmed profitable trades on front-side moves while filtering out choppy, false-breakout periods. He emphasizes that MACD is one tool among many, used alongside price action analysis and volume confirmation, not as a standalone trading signal. Ross notes that he removes MACD from his charts during hot bull markets when setups are clean and straightforward, but reintroduces it during periods of heightened market chop to maintain trading discipline. The video reinforces that technical indicators are only valuable when used consistently as part of a trader's routine, and that the combination of MACD, VWAP, and price pattern recognition provides the best risk management in uncertain market environments.

FILE 0793 | TYPE: No Trades

NO-TRADE SUMMARY:
Ross provides a detailed breakdown of the dead cat bounce pattern, a technical setup that occurs when stocks experience sharp, severe declines followed by quick recoveries from the lows. Using MegL as the primary case study, he explains that the pattern emerges after extreme sell-offs—such as an IPO that climbs to $250 and plummets to $8—when the stock snaps back with a bounce off the lows. The dead cat bounce is distinct from a full recovery; it represents a temporary recovery with limited upside potential unless additional catalysts emerge. Ross outlines the pattern identification process across both daily and intraday timeframes, noting that the first daily candle to make a new high after a substantial sell-off is the key technical confirmation. He discusses position sizing and entry strategy, explaining how watching level two order flow helps identify when large sellers are exhausted, creating the opportunity to enter as the stock bounces. Ross emphasizes the importance of patience in waiting for the bounce to confirm before committing capital, as false bottoms and continued selling pressure are common risks. The video addresses the psychology of trading extreme reversals, noting that traders often prematurely buy the dip before the stock has truly stabilized. He explains how MACD divergence, volume profile shifts, and support level holds validate the setup's viability for larger moves.

FILE 0796 | TYPE: No Trades
---

NO-TRADE SUMMARY:
Ross reflects on a day of trader rehab following a significant emotional loss, evaluating his adherence to six core trading rules during recovery. After suffering a $20,000 loss on the previous day due to emotional trading and refusing to accept small losses, Ross implements strict restrictions on himself including capping position size at 5,000 shares and limiting daily trades. He discusses the psychological and tactical framework of trader rehab, starting with acknowledging heightened emotional state, applying position size and trade count restrictions, practicing mindfulness and meditation, and building a small cushion before removing restrictions. The day turned highly profitable, with one primary trade on GX delivering the majority of gains despite the restrictions, illustrating how smaller position sizes can protect against catastrophic losses while still allowing recovery. Ross emphasizes that restriction is temporary and purposeful—the goal is not to eliminate profits but to rebuild confidence and break patterns of revenge trading or FOMO-driven decisions. He explains the importance of not lifting restrictions prematurely despite a profitable day, as the real test is demonstrating consistent discipline over several trading days. The video addresses the broader concept of trading in different psychological states, distinguishing between hot markets where aggressive positioning is appropriate and cold markets where trader rehab discipline is required. Ross reinforces that all traders experience drawdowns and emotional spirals, and that recognizing these states and implementing systematic solutions is the hallmark of professional trading.

NO-TRADE SUMMARY:
Ross presents an educational overview of trading around circuit breaker halts, specifically the dip-and-rip pattern that occurs when stocks resume trading after halting upward. When a stock halts due to a 10% price move within five minutes, it briefly pauses trading. Upon resumption, Ross explains that shorts often take profit, pushing the stock down momentarily, while new buyers jump in for the continuation, creating a quick dip followed by ripping higher. The pattern is particularly tradeable because the halt itself signals extreme volatility and genuine demand, differentiating it from quiet consolidations. Ross discusses halt-specific strategies, noting that multiple consecutive halts upward indicate sustained buying pressure, while a halt downward suggests potential shorting pressure. He reviews various halt patterns and their historical profitability, emphasizing that halt resumptions offer clearly defined risk levels and strong continuation potential. The video covers market conditions required for halt trading, noting that while it can occur in any market regime, the clearest opportunities come during hot market conditions with significant overall volume and volatility. Ross stresses the importance of quick decision-making and tight stop losses, as halt moves can reverse rapidly. The educational segment references specific examples of stocks that halted multiple times before major moves, illustrating how recognizing halt patterns contributes to identifying early-stage momentum moves.

NO-TRADE SUMMARY:
Ross provides an in-depth analysis of Trump coin, the meme coin launched by Donald Trump, focusing on the mechanics of supply and demand that created a $60 billion market capitalization virtually overnight. He explains the fundamental difference between Trump's official coin and unofficial Trump-related tokens, noting that the backing of a prominent figure drives demand concentration. The coin was created with a fixed supply of one billion coins, with Trump retaining 80% and allowing the remaining 20% to freely trade. Ross demonstrates that the paper wealth creation—approximately $50 billion in Trump's unrealized gains—is only realized if he sells, and that attempting to sell would collapse the price since there is insufficient trading volume to absorb such a massive position. He draws parallels to other meme coins and previous instances of insider dumps, discussing the risk-reward dynamics of holding positions in coins backed by single individuals. Ross addresses the regulatory and ethical questions surrounding meme coins, noting persistent scam activity and questionable practices in the crypto space. He discusses the practical trading implications, explaining how MACD crossovers and technical analysis apply to crypto assets, and his own avoidance of trading the position due to exchange counterparty risk concerns. The video touches on how cryptocurrency performance and volatility can influence equity market conditions, particularly as institutions and retail traders position for potential regulatory changes. Ross emphasizes the importance of understanding supply dynamics and the dangers of chasing extreme moves based on FOMO.

SUMMARY:
Ross finished the morning up only $811, his smallest green day of the month despite heavy trading activity. A day of light momentum tested Ross's discipline after a string of larger wins earlier in the week. SMIT was the leading gapper, gapping up 45% from $3.43 to break the premarket high at $3.70, presenting a textbook gap-and-go setup. Ross entered at $3.90-$3.95 and initially captured $400 in profit scaling at $4.05-$4.07, a solid base hit. However, the stock then pulled back dramatically and dipped below the initial entry, triggering a reversal candle that signaled selling pressure. Rather than defend the trade, Ross exited for a small $100 loss on the second attempt. Critically, he attempted a third entry as the stock consolidated, chasing what appeared to be a micro pullback breakout. This proved to be a false breakout—the stock flushed dramatically to $2.52, and Ross was stopped out for a $1,600 loss, his first significant daily loss in a week. The trade revealed an important lesson: after two attempts on the same stock, adding conviction on a third try is often overconfidence. MTSL, MATPE, and TRT provided small wins ranging from $400-$1,200 on gap scanner setups, but without a home-run trade, the day became a grinding session requiring 15+ trades to produce the $811 profit. By late morning, recognizing the market lacked hot momentum and his small green days preceded losses, Ross made the mature decision to stop trading and protect his weekly gains rather than risk a drawdown. This demonstrated significant growth: six years ago, $811 would have felt exceptional, but trading discipline sometimes means walking away early when conditions deteriorate.

WORX was the clear leading gapper, gapping up 22% pre-market on news and presenting Ross's primary opportunity. He executed the classic premarket-scan-to-breakout setup: watching the stock for a break of the $7.50 premarket high. When the bell rang, WORX shot immediately to $8.76, triggering Ross's breakout strategy. However, his market order received only a 1,010-share partial fill instead of his intended 3,000-share position—initially frustrating but ultimately protective given the stock's subsequent volatility. Ross built his position through planned adds at dips, specifically at $7.87, $8.21, and entering the halt at $8.76. The stock eventually reached $9.70 but Ross got mentally caught between two accounts: he added 9,000 shares in the Centrepointe margin account at $8.76 thinking the stock would halt again and push to $11+. When the high came at $9.70 instead, he was overextended. However, avoiding panic, he waited for the first one-minute candle to make a new high post-dip. When it didn't, he exited, limiting losses to $3,200 in the margin account while banking $9,600 in the main IRA account. CLPS was a secondary trade providing $3,500: entered at $16.50 as it broke above the previous day's range, rode the momentum to $18.19, and exited on the squeeze. The win-loss math: eight consecutive green days pushed February-to-date profit to $68,000 with eleven trading days remaining—on pace to exceed his $100,000 monthly goal.

NO-TRADE SUMMARY:
Ross presents a detailed recap of an emotionally-driven trading day that resulted in a $20,000 loss, serving as a case study in behavioral trading errors and the psychological spiral that can derail even experienced traders. The day began promisingly with early gains, but Ross broke his own rules by refusing to accept a small loss on the first trade, instead holding and adding to a losing position in hopes of recovery. This revenge-trading mentality escalated his position size and increased emotional stakes, leading to panic selling at the worst possible time. Ross explains how the loss sequence triggered a chain reaction: initial small loss, refusal to accept it, over-leverage attempt to recover, and final capitulation at maximum pain. He emphasizes that the emotional hijacking that followed the loss—where all trading judgment temporarily disappeared—is a documented psychological state that requires systematic intervention. Ross discusses how a series of previous red days heightened emotional vulnerability and reduced his psychological resilience, making him more prone to emotional decisions. He contrasts the day's losses against his monthly and yearly performance to provide context, noting that while $20,000 is significant, it represents less than 1% of his year-to-date profits. The video functions as a teaching moment about recognizing emotional states, understanding trigger patterns, and implementing mechanical rules to override emotional decisions. Ross concludes by announcing trader rehab as his response, demonstrating that even professional traders must reset and rebuild confidence after significant emotional losses.

As energy stocks broadly lifted on USO strength, Ross added at $9.50 and $9.68 before breakout through $10. When INDO squeezed to $10.51, Ross scaled into momentum, capturing $10,000 (entire day's gain). Session exemplified disciplined trading: exceeded goal and immediately stopped rather than forcing additional trades. His year-to-date average $4,600 made $10,000 a strong 2.2x day.

SUMMARY:
Ross finished up $1,045 despite frustration from missing INPX's explosive move from $5.17→$5.89. Day exemplifies tension between disciplined risk management and FOMO. INPX was leading gapper (up 10%, 9M float), executing classic playbook: watched premarket high break (~$4.10), entered $4.41-$4.50, rode first pop to $8.50, scaled out +$1,000. Re-entered micro-pullback dip at $7.50-$7.75 expecting pattern repeat, but stock reversed hard for -$600 loss. Frustrated but observant, Ross drew ascending support line through $5.10. When consolidated lower, he re-entered anticipating bounce, added at $5.10, rode back through $9.00+ (high $9.50+), capturing another +$1,000. However, after locking profits on third trade, INPX continued to $5.89. Ross had two "threshold triggers": (1) max daily loss limit ($5k account cap), (2) "give back 50% of gains" rule. After hitting second rule giving back half profits on failed dip trade, forced to stop trading. ADAP was only loss: second leading gapper but opened weak. Ross aggressively sized 6k-13k shares thinking it would follow INPX. It didn't, -$2,400 loss. Session ended with reframed perspective: discipline saved him from revenge-trading after failed INPX dip, but watching INPX run to $5.89 created FOMO. Meta-lesson: treading water with small profits when conditions deteriorate late in day often proves wisest.

NO-TRADE SUMMARY:
Ross presents a detailed replay of a trading day where FOMO (fear of missing out) behavior cost him $23,000 in losses, turning what should have been a $2,900 profitable day into a significant drawdown. After multiple small green trades throughout the day, Ross held a comfortable profit but then violated his own discipline by taking an oversized position on a lower-quality setup. Despite warning signs—including poor daily chart configuration and resistance levels—Ross entered the trade driven by emotional urgency rather than technical conviction. When the trade moved against him, he refused to accept the loss, instead holding and averaging down, doubling his position in hopes of recovery. The stock ultimately liquidated him at maximum loss, erasing all daily gains and creating a net loss. Ross reflects on the pattern of decisions that led to the failure: hours of successful, disciplined trading followed by one emotional decision that reversed the entire day's results. He commits to trader rehab starting Monday, implementing restrictions including a maximum daily loss trigger, limited share size, and a cap on trades per day. Ross discusses how the end-of-month pressure, combined with recent big winning days, created a false sense of invincibility that lowered his defensive guardrails. The video serves as a visceral reminder that trading success depends not on individual trade outcomes but on following systematic rules consistently, and that one undisciplined decision can eliminate the profits from dozens of proper trades.

Strategy: (1) first trade standard highest, looking for 20-30 cent potential, (2) if first trade goes red, take smaller subsequent trades to minimize damage, (3) once back to breakeven or slightly green, reassess market and decide whether to continue or sit out. His key insight: hot markets and cold markets require entirely different approaches; traders who excel in both are rare.

His trading approach during hot markets: identify breaking-news stocks with 0.5-5M float, enter early with small size, scale into winners with MACD confirmation, but take profits into strength rather than hoping for +$10/share moves that rarely materialize. The cryptographic cycles of market volatility (crypto bull/bear, Fed policy, geopolitical tariffs) drive overall momentum, but daily discipline remains the differentiator between profitability and ruin.

The context included his recovery from a $44,000 loss early in the month by implementing Trader Rehab—a six-step process (acknowledge emotional state, apply account restrictions, practice mindfulness, implement specific rules like maximum share count, rebuild confidence gradually, scale up only after recovery). He discussed how consecutive winning days (23 in a row) created complacency that led to the big loss, and how breaking that streak triggered additional emotional loss-chasing. The message centered on the skill of losing properly as fundamental to long-term success, more important than winning big.

He outlined his five-pillar stock selection framework: (1) Price ($2-$20 range, sweetspot $5-$10), (2) Percentage up today (minimum 25%, prefer top three gainers), (3) Relative Volume (RV, minimum 5x), (4) News catalyst (yes or no), (5) Float (under 20M shares, under 5M preferred). He walked through two hypothetical stock scenarios to show why a $21 stock with 26% gain and 19M float is not worth trading despite meeting technical criteria, whereas a $5 stock at 75% with 1.9M float is highly tradeable. His approach in cold markets is to tighten criteria further (fewer total trades, focus on lower float exclusively). He discussed ATNF as a case study of a stock that met criteria but whose recent history of false breakouts made him hesitant to commit fully, eventually missing a 72% move but avoiding risk. This represented his philosophy: discipline in stock selection over frequency, and better to miss moves than to catch them at poor risk-reward ratios.

SUMMARY:
This episode was primarily a case study analysis of VERB (up 400%) rather than a personal trading recap, though it contained discussion of personal trades from Trader Rehab Day 3. VERB served as an example of why Ross does not seriously trade sub-$1.00 stocks despite explosive percentage gains. The core issue: a penny stock moving from $0.20 to $0.30 requires 10,000 shares to capture a $60 profit potential (before commissions), whereas a $5-$10 stock only requires 10,000 shares to make the same profit for a smaller dollar move. The math disadvantages penny stocks: they trade in tiny increments (down to 1/100th of a penny), meaning 100 price ticks are needed to move 1 cent, versus stocks over $1 which trade in whole increments. Additionally, panic flushes in penny stocks cause poor fills if trying to unload large positions. Ross watched VERB from $0.30 premarket squeeze to $0.92 intraday (over 200%+) but chose not to trade it, explaining his risk management reasons: unable to size up to the 100,000 shares needed for meaningful profits while controlling risk. His personal trades (LMFA, AISP) showed controlled position sizing (5,000-6,000 share max) as part of his Trader Rehab recovery, ending $1,929.50 on the day. The VERB case study was designed to educate viewers on why he focuses on the $5-$10 price zone for optimal risk-reward rather than chasing penny stock parabolas.

Key insight: large amount of selling hitting with limited visible bids but price not breaking lower = evidence of hidden accumulation underneath (typical of institutional/large hedge fund buying). Discussed technical indicator (gravestone doji on red volume) that suggested reversal, but level-two told different story (hidden buyer overrode bearish candlestick). Ross did not trade KRTX despite perfect setup recognition because: (1) stock opened at $30/share—too expensive for small account challenge rules ($5-$10 sweet spot), (2) spreads were extremely wide ($1.90 spread on $55 bid-ask), (3) institutional-size buyer suggested long-term accumulation, not day-trade scalp. Goldman Sachs price target $100+. Educational value: perfect example of how level-two reveals true supply/demand not visible on price charts alone. No trade taken; observation and learning only.

NO-TRADE SUMMARY:
This video is a monthly performance review for January 2020, a session Ross normally reserves for his Warrior Pro students during his first-week-of-the-month mentoring session. He shares it publicly because January was a particularly instructive roller coaster. The net result was essentially breakeven across his main trading and IRA accounts -- down $133 in total -- while spending over $12,000 in commissions, a personal monthly record that he called embarrassing. His gross profit exceeded $70,000 in winning trades but was entirely consumed by losses from over-trading.

Ross identifies overtrading as the core failure: he took 260 trades averaging 175,000 shares per day, with accuracy dropping to 57% against his historical average of 66%. He traded three accounts simultaneously -- main, IRA, and TD Ameritrade -- allowing losses in one account to go unacknowledged while he continued risking in another. He also violated his rule against afternoon trading, losing approximately $10,000 in afternoon sessions alone, motivated by the desire to recover morning losses. A max-loss limit set at -$1,000 paradoxically caused a larger loss on one occasion by making him hesitant to cut a losing first trade, so he raised it to -$5,000.

The key takeaways Ross commits to for February: no afternoon trading, fewer and higher-quality trades (quality over quantity), trading one account at a time, and resisting the psychological pull of monthly PnL benchmarking. He adds a sticky note to his monitor reading "don't be careless" as a pre-trading ritual. He notes that his best trade of the month -- a $20,000 winner on TWMC -- was ultimately just bailing him out from impulsive low-quality trades rather than being a net positive contribution. The session includes a deep discussion of commission economics, emotional conditioning, and the cyclical nature of aggressive trading patterns at the start of each new month or year.
